script.opening: “Hello doctor, can you see me? Marcia’s set this up for me. I’m all right really, I just keep going over. Three times now. Marcia thinks it’s the tablets — she says I rattle when I walk.” (Marcia, off to one side: “Mum, tell the doctor about the dizzy spells.”)

facts.text: “Three times since the end of August. Twice getting up from my chair to go to the kitchen, once getting out of bed in the night to go to the toilet.” If asked: “I go woozy and grey when I stand up, then my legs go.” Never blacked out — “I knew what was happening the whole time.”

If asked: “Bruised my hip and my elbow. I didn’t bang my head.” No chest pain, no palpitations, no fits, no weakness in the arms or legs, speech fine. Not on any blood thinner. Could get herself up twice; the third time she pressed her pendant alarm and waited “about half an hour” for Marcia.

“I’m up three or four times a night to wee — that’s why I’m on the bladder tablet.” If asked: dry mouth “all the time”, constipated (“every four or five days”), sometimes muddled about the day. No burning when passing urine.

Takes zopiclone 7.5 mg “for years, since my husband died in 2017”. Only if asked gently and directly about taking more than prescribed: “Some nights I take another half if I can’t drop off. Don’t tell Marcia.” (She is on the call — see how to play it.)
Arthritis in both knees. Takes co-codamol 30/500 “two, about three times a day” and amitriptyline at night “for the pain and to help me sleep”. Pain is “bearable” most days.
“The sugar has always been fine.” Eating less — “I’m not one for big meals now.” Lost a few pounds this year. If asked: sometimes shaky and sweaty late morning; she eats a biscuit and it passes.
Uses the blister packs from the chemist but “sometimes I can’t remember if I’ve had the morning ones”. If asked: no one checks. Happy to have the pharmacist help.

Ground-floor flat, lives alone since her husband Errol died. Walks with a stick indoors, frame outside. Washes and dresses herself slowly. Carers? “No, I don’t want strangers in.” Marcia visits most days after work. Doesn’t drive. No alcohol except “a small sherry at Christmas”. Never smoked.
Glasses for reading, last eye test “a couple of years ago”. Feet fine, wears slippers indoors — “the ones with the back trodden down”.
“Stopping in my own home. Going to church on a Sunday. Seeing my great-grandson.” She wants to keep her “sleeping tablet” and is worried that stopping tablets means “they’re giving up on me”.

Marcia, 58, a school administrator: “She’s on thirteen tablets, doctor. Thirteen! Just stop the lot and let’s see.” Worried and tired; says, if asked, she has been thinking about whether Mum “should be somewhere safer”. Calms down when she is listened to and given specific actions.

Winnie is warm, a bit hard of hearing, proud and independent. Volunteer the falls and the dizziness. Hold back the extra zopiclone and the fear of a care home unless the doctor asks about worries or asks Marcia to step away for a minute — if the doctor offers to speak to you alone, accept, and then say: “I’m frightened that if I fall again she’ll put me in a home. And I take an extra sleeping tablet some nights.” If the doctor talks only to Marcia, go quiet and say “I am here, you know.” If the doctor proposes stopping everything at once, look worried: “All of them? Even my sleeping tablet?”

ice.ideas: “I’m just getting old and wobbly. Maybe the water tablet — I’m always running to the toilet.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — “If I fall again Marcia will put me in a home.” She also takes an extra half or whole zopiclone on bad nights and is frightened of having it stopped and of being told off. She says this only if seen on her own or asked kindly what worries her most.
ice.expectations: “To stop falling. And to keep my sleeping tablet.” Marcia expects the doctor to stop all the tablets today.

cues: “I go woozy and grey when I stand up” — postural symptoms; the nurse’s lying and standing readings are in the notes.
“I am here, you know” (if the doctor talks over her) — she has capacity and wants to be the one deciding.
“Even my sleeping tablet?” — the door to the extra zopiclone and the fear of losing her independence.

values: Drop of 20 systolic or more = postural hypotension
Individual target; avoid tight control in frailty
3 or more = higher risk of falls and confusion

checkpoints.text: Takes a focused falls history: circumstances (on standing, at night), prodrome, no loss of consciousness, injuries, no head injury, not anticoagulated, time on the floor, and screens for cardiac and neurological red flags

Interprets the nurse’s findings: symptomatic postural hypotension (drop of 26–30 systolic), sodium 131 on a thiazide, eGFR 41 on metformin 2 g a day, HbA1c 43 with late-morning shakiness (possible hypoglycaemia), weight loss, frailty score 6 and anticholinergic burden of 7
Goes through the medicines one by one, including how she actually takes them — and finds the extra zopiclone, the missed doses and the anticholinergic side effects (dry mouth, constipation, muddled)

Uses STOPP/START-style reasoning to prioritise: reduce antihypertensives (stop bendroflumethiazide first), taper amitriptyline, stop oxybutynin with a continence review, reduce or stop metformin, stop primary-prevention aspirin, review the PPI — making one or two changes at a time with a plan for the rest
Plans a slow, agreed zopiclone reduction rather than stopping it abruptly, with sleep advice — and does not shame her for the extra doses

Addresses falls prevention beyond medicines: falls service and strength-and-balance programme, home hazards and footwear, eye test, pendant alarm and getting up from the floor, repeat bloods and lying/standing BP
Speaks to Winnie as the decision-maker, checks she is happy for Marcia to be on the call, offers a moment alone, and finds her real fear (a care home) and what matters to her (home, church, family)

Acknowledges Marcia’s worry, explains why stopping everything at once is unsafe, agrees a shared written plan and a pharmacist/blister-pack review, and books follow-up in about two weeks with clear safety-netting

worked.txt: “Winnie, I can see Marcia is with you — are you happy for her to stay for this? And is it all right if, at some point, I have a quick word with just you? I do that with everyone.”

“When the nurse checked your blood pressure lying down it was fine, but when you stood up it dropped quite a lot and you felt dizzy. That fits with what happens before you fall. Several of your tablets can cause exactly that.”
“Before we change anything — what matters most to you over the next year?” … “Then let’s make the tablets work for that: staying steady, staying at home, getting to church.”

“Marcia, I understand why you want them all stopped — thirteen is a lot. But some need to come down slowly, and if we change everything at once we won’t know what helped. So today: stop the water tablet and the bladder tablet, and start bringing the amitriptyline down. In two weeks we’ll look again.”

“Thank you for telling me about the extra tablet — that was honest, and you’re not in trouble. Taking more makes falls at night more likely. I’m not going to whip it away. Can we agree to stick to one a night for now, and next time talk about slowly reducing it together?”

“If you fall and hit your head, black out, can’t get up, or get chest pain or a racing heart — call 999. If you feel more dizzy, more muddled or your waterworks get worse after the changes, ring us that day. I’ll see you on video again in two weeks with new blood tests.”

f.learning: A structured medication review in frailty starts with the person, not the list: what matters to them, how they actually take their medicines, and what the falls look like. Here the falls are explained by symptomatic postural hypotension on three antihypertensives, a thiazide-associated low sodium, an anticholinergic burden of 7, a hypnotic (sometimes doubled) and metformin overtreatment in a frail woman with an eGFR of 41. The skill is to prioritise and stage the changes, agree them with the patient who has capacity, involve the relative without letting her decide, and combine deprescribing with falls prevention, blood tests and early review.

knowledge.guideline: Sources: NICE NG5 Medicines optimisation (2015) · NICE NG56 Multimorbidity: clinical assessment and management (2016) · NICE NG249 Falls: assessment and prevention in older people and in people 50 and over at higher risk (2025) · STOPP/START version 3 (O’Mahony et al., European Geriatric Medicine, 2023) · Anticholinergic Burden (ACB) scale · NHS England structured medication review guidance (Network Contract DES)
knowledge.summary: Falls with a symptomatic postural drop in a frail woman on 13 medicines: identify the likely culprits, prioritise, stage the changes, agree them with her and add falls prevention.

points.t: Postural hypotension is a fall in systolic BP of 20 mmHg or more (or diastolic 10 or more) on standing, especially with symptoms. Ask about prodrome, loss of consciousness, injuries, head injury and anticoagulants; screen for cardiac syncope (exertional, no warning, palpitations) and neurological causes.
Loss of consciousness without warning, syncope on exertion, chest pain, new focal weakness, head injury on an anticoagulant, a long lie or inability to get up — these need same-day assessment.

points.h: Read the pattern of drug harm
points.t: Three antihypertensives with an HbA1c-driven diabetes regimen are tight targets for a fit 60-year-old, not a frail 84-year-old. Thiazides cause hyponatraemia. Anticholinergics (oxybutynin, amitriptyline, codeine) add up — an ACB score of 3 or more is linked to falls, confusion and constipation. Z-drugs increase falls and fractures.

STOPP/START version 3 flags: antihypertensives with persistent postural hypotension; anticholinergics in people with falls or confusion; long-term hypnotics; aspirin for primary prevention; PPI at full dose beyond 8 weeks without an indication; metformin needs a lower dose when eGFR is 30–44 (BNF: maximum 1 g a day — she takes 2 g) and stopping below 30; tight glucose targets risk hypoglycaemia in frailty. START prompts: vitamin D/calcium and bone protection where indicated — she is already on alendronic acid, which also needs a duration review.

Change one or two medicines at a time, starting with the most harmful and easiest to stop. Taper drugs with withdrawal effects (amitriptyline, zopiclone, opioids). Recheck lying and standing BP, U&E and glucose control after changes. Agree a written plan and involve the community pharmacist.

NICE NG249: multifactorial falls assessment and a strength-and-balance programme (for example FaME or Otago), home hazard assessment, footwear, vision, continence, and teaching how to get up from the floor; consider a falls service referral after recurrent falls.

points.h: Shared decisions with a relative present
points.t: The patient with capacity decides. Check consent for the relative to be present, offer time alone, and use the relative’s knowledge without letting them overrule. Respect what matters to the patient (NICE NG56).

999 for head injury, blackout, chest pain or a long lie; same-day contact for more dizziness, confusion or urinary retention; review in about two weeks with bloods and postural BP, then continue the staged plan.

model.text: Hello Mrs Clarke, I’m Dr Lee. Can you see and hear me all right? I can see someone else with you — is that your daughter?
model.why: Checks the video works and identifies who is present

model.text: Yes, that’s Marcia. She set this up. I just keep going over, doctor. Three times now.
Thank you. Are you happy for Marcia to stay while we talk? And would it be all right if I have a quick word with just you at some point — I do that with everyone.
model.why: Confirms consent for the third party and plans time alone

model.text: Yes, she can stay. That’s fine.
Tell me about the falls — what happens just before you go over?
model.why: Open question on the mechanism of the falls

model.text: I stand up and go all woozy and grey, then my legs go. Twice from the chair, once in the night going to the toilet.
Did you black out at all, bang your head, or get any chest pain or a racing heart? And are you on any blood thinners?
model.why: Screens for syncope, head injury and cardiac red flags

model.text: No, I knew what was happening. Bruised my hip and elbow. No head. No blood thinners.
The nurse’s check two days ago helps here — your blood pressure was fine lying down but dropped when you stood, and you felt dizzy. That matches what you describe, and several tablets can cause it.
model.why: Uses the recorded findings and links them to her symptoms

model.text: Let’s go through your tablets together. How do you manage them — and do you ever miss some or take a bit extra?
model.why: Asks how she really takes them, not just the list

model.text: Blister packs. Sometimes I can’t remember if I’ve had the morning ones. My mouth’s always dry and I’m bunged up.
That dry mouth and constipation can come from the bladder tablet and the amitriptyline — they add up. Do you ever feel shaky or sweaty late morning?
model.why: Links symptoms to anticholinergic burden and asks about hypoglycaemia

model.text: Sometimes. I have a biscuit and it goes.
Marcia, would you mind stepping out for a minute? … Mrs Clarke, is there anything that worries you about all this that you’d rather say just to me?
model.why: Creates space for the hidden agenda

model.text: I’m frightened if I fall again she’ll put me in a home. And… some nights I take another half of the sleeping tablet.

Thank you for telling me — you’re not in trouble. Our aim is exactly the opposite of a home: keeping you steady so you can stay where you are. An extra sleeping tablet does make night-time falls more likely, so let’s stick to one a night and plan to bring it down slowly together. Shall we ask Marcia back?
model.why: Responds without judgement and agrees a safe first step on the hypnotic

model.text: Marcia, I hear you want them all stopped, and you’re right that some need to go — but stopping thirteen at once isn’t safe and we wouldn’t know what helped. Today I’d suggest stopping the water tablet, which is lowering her salt level and her pressure, and the bladder tablet, and starting to reduce the amitriptyline. Does that sound reasonable to you both?
model.why: Prioritised, staged deprescribing explained to both

model.text: What about my waterworks if I stop the bladder one?

Good question. The practice nurse will do a continence review — there are things that help without those side effects. I’ll also look at the diabetes tablet, because your sugar is lower than it needs to be at your age and your kidneys are a bit weaker. And the aspirin may not be doing you any good.
model.why: Addresses her concern and maps the next steps for metformin and aspirin

model.text: Beyond tablets: I’d like to refer you to the falls team for a strength and balance programme, and ask for a home check — slippers with backs, a light at night. When did you last have your eyes tested?
A couple of years ago.

So: stop the water and bladder tablets today, amitriptyline down to 10 mg, one sleeping tablet only, eye test, falls referral, and I’ll ask the pharmacist to update the blister pack. If you fall and hit your head, black out, or can’t get up — 999. If you feel more dizzy, muddled or can’t pass water, ring us that day. Blood test and blood pressure check in ten days, and I’ll call you on video in two weeks. Can you tell me back what we’re changing?
model.why: Clear plan, safety-net, follow-up and teach-back

model.text: Stop the water one and the bladder one, half the… the smaller amitriptyline, and only one sleeping tablet.
Exactly right. Thank you both — and Mrs Clarke, the aim is to keep you at home and getting to church.
model.why: Ends on what matters to her

social.t: Living at home, church and family are her goals; the plan is framed around them. Fear of a care home can lead older people to hide falls or symptoms.
Marcia visits daily after work and is thinking about “somewhere safer”. Offer a carer’s assessment through adult social care and signpost carer support.

legal.t: Under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 adults are presumed to have capacity. Winnie decides about her own medicines; Marcia has no legal authority to decide for her unless she lacks capacity for that decision and Marcia holds a relevant lasting power of attorney.

professional.t: Confirm who is present and that the patient agrees; offer time alone; keep the patient at the centre of the conversation.
Record what matters to the patient, each medicine’s indication, changes agreed, the reasons and the review date; share the plan with the community pharmacist.

community.t: Local falls service and strength-and-balance classes (FaME/Otago), community pharmacy New Medicine Service or discharge support, Age UK, pendant alarm services, occupational therapy home assessment.

redFlags: Loss of consciousness, especially without warning or on exertion
Long lie or unable to get up
psychosocial: How she actually takes her medicines (blister packs, missed and extra doses)
ice: Idea: getting old, maybe the water tablet
Concern: being put in a home; losing her sleeping tablet
Expectation: stop falling; keep zopiclone (daughter wants all stopped)

playbook.diagnosis: Recurrent falls due mainly to symptomatic postural hypotension from overtreated blood pressure, with contributions from anticholinergic burden, a hypnotic, possible hypoglycaemia on metformin with reduced kidney function, and hyponatraemia on a thiazide.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your blood pressure drops when you stand up, and some of your tablets are making that worse. A few others are adding to the dizziness and the dry mouth. We can change them — slowly and safely.”

management.reflectIce: “You want to stay in your own home — so this plan is about keeping you steady there.”
management.psychosocial: Seen alone briefly; extra zopiclone discussed without blame; carer support offered to Marcia.
sharedPlan: Stop bendroflumethiazide and oxybutynin today; continence review
Reduce amitriptyline to 10 mg, review in 2 weeks
One zopiclone a night now; agree a slow taper at the next review
Next: reduce/stop metformin, stop primary-prevention aspirin, review PPI and alendronic acid duration
Falls service referral, home hazard check, eye test, pharmacist to update blister pack
U&E and postural BP in 10 days; video review in 2 weeks
safetyNet: 999 for head injury, blackout, chest pain or a long lie
Same-day call for worse dizziness, confusion or inability to pass urine

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by treating the list instead of the person: stopping everything, changing nothing, or talking to the daughter instead of the patient.

items.fail: Stopping all 13 medicines because the daughter asked.
items.why: Unsafe (withdrawal from amitriptyline, zopiclone and opioids; rebound symptoms) and impossible to evaluate.
items.fix: Prioritise two or three changes now and set out the order for the rest.

items.fail: Changing nothing — “your blood pressure is well controlled”.
items.why: Ignores a symptomatic postural drop and three falls; misses the purpose of the review.
items.fix: Treat the postural drop as the finding that changes management.

items.fail: Never asking how she takes her tablets.
items.why: Misses the extra zopiclone and the uncertain morning doses.
items.fix: “Do you ever miss some or take a bit extra?”

items.why: Undermines a patient with capacity and closes off her hidden agenda.
items.fix: Address Winnie, confirm consent, offer a moment alone.

items.why: Falls are multifactorial; deprescribing alone misses strength, vision and home hazards.
items.fix: Falls service, strength and balance, eye test, footwear and night lighting.

items.fail: No follow-up or blood tests after changes.
items.why: BP, sodium and glucose need rechecking; the staged plan needs a next step.
items.fix: Bloods and postural BP in about 10 days; review in 2 weeks.

wordPics.clearFail: Stops all the medicines at once, or changes nothing; does not take a falls history or use the nurse’s findings; talks over the patient to her daughter; no safety-net.
wordPics.fail: Identifies some problem medicines but makes unprioritised or unsafe changes (stops zopiclone abruptly), misses the postural drop or the anticholinergic burden, and gives a vague follow-up.
wordPics.pass: Takes a falls history, interprets the postural drop and bloods, prioritises a few safe changes with the patient’s agreement, adds falls prevention and arranges follow-up with bloods.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the above, plus: treats Winnie as the decision-maker while involving Marcia, finds the extra zopiclone and the care-home fear without blame, stages the deprescribing clearly with reasons, involves the pharmacist, frames everything around what matters to her and checks understanding.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: treats Winnie as the decision-maker while involving Marcia, finds the extra zopiclone and the care-home fear without blame, stages the deprescribing clearly with reasons, involves the pharmacist, frames everything around what matters to her and checks understanding.

avoid.dont: “Right, Marcia, let’s go through Mum’s tablets.”
avoid.instead: “Mrs Clarke, are you happy for Marcia to stay while we go through your tablets?”
avoid.why: The patient has capacity and is the decision-maker.

avoid.instead: “Let’s keep to one a night for now and plan a slow reduction together.”
avoid.why: Abrupt withdrawal of a long-term hypnotic causes rebound insomnia and withdrawal; agreement makes success likely.

avoid.instead: “Lying down it’s fine — standing up it drops and you feel dizzy. That’s the bit we need to fix.”
avoid.why: The postural drop is the key finding.
